name: Manifold Trace
observation:
Looking down through the deck grating, a single bright slug of hot coolant crawls south along a dark channel lane painted into the glow bed at x=+2.9 (hard against the east side of the pit, directly beneath the gauge bank). The lane carries SIX numbered station marks at z = -2.25, -1.35, -0.45, +0.45, +1.35, +2.25 — each a dark stencilled digit ~0.68m tall burned into the coolant pool, legible through the grating. The slug runs z = -3.3 -> +3.3 once per loop (T = 18s), 0.367 m/s, reaching a new station every 2.455s, then recirculating off the dark north end.

On the east wall above it, the four existing gauge quads (y=1.5, z = -1.35/-0.45/+0.45/+1.35) each carry a needle that now sits IDLE at a seeded rest angle on the left of the dial — no wobble. Once per loop, and only once, each gauge VENTS: its needle slams across to full right deflection over 0.35s, pins there for 0.5s, and falls back over 0.35s. Four gauges, four vents, four different moments in the 18s loop.

From the west aisle (standing just east of the piston bank, x approx -2.4) the gauge bank sits at -1.2 degrees elevation and the numbered channel at -24.5 degrees depression — both inside the camera's 62-degree vertical FOV. The player sees the needle slam and the slug's position in the SAME frame, without turning. That sightline is the whole reason the channel is on the east side of the pit and not the middle.

Behind all of it, the flywheel keeps chopping the glow as it always did, now re-timed to exactly 18 strobes per loop, so the room is its own metronome and the vents can be counted in flashes.
deduction:
Each gauge vents at the exact instant the coolant slug is centred over ONE specific numbered station — the same station, every loop, forever.

The "oh, THAT's what's happening" is the moment the player stops reading the gauges as instruments and realises they are announcements. The gauges have no names, no units, no scale — the game has always framed that as a missing lookup table. It isn't. A gauge that is unlabelled and only ever does one thing, once, at one moment, is not measuring anything: it is pointing. The needle is not a reading, it is a finger, and what it points at is on the floor.

Two things make this a deduction rather than a transcription:
1. Only FOUR of the six stations are ever named. Two digits sit in the lane the whole session and never belong to the answer. So the player cannot read the lane north-to-south and type six-minus-two; they must catch the coincidence to know which four are live and which gauge owns each.
2. The gauge->station map is deliberately non-monotonic (seed-enforced), so the four live stations in wall order are scrambled — noticing "the north gauge takes a middle station" is what kills the guess that the two banks simply line up.

Everything else in the room is honest noise with a period that divides T, so nothing drifts into a false coincidence that never resolves: pistons at T/9 = 2.0s in a seeded firing order, flywheel at T/3 = 6.0s per revolution. A player who fixates on the pistons sees a real, stable rhythm that simply has no gauge attached to it.

Note on determinism: the answer is defined as the state of one object at the instant another object does something, so it is invariant under any global time offset. Two players doubled into the same chamber with different mount times see the slug in different places at the same wall-clock moment, but they read the SAME four digits. The puzzle therefore needs no shared clock. Passing the run clock is still recommended so they can talk about it, but correctness does not depend on it.
neighbourKeyRole:
The neighbour holds MANIFOLD ORDER: the four gauge glyph-pairs listed in the order the readings must be entered — for example "▮◇ , ○▮ , △△ , ◇▲". It contains no digits, no station numbers and no positions, so it can never be the answer.

It gates the last step and only the last step. The Engine player does all the observation unaided and ends up holding a complete map — {○▮:2, ◇▲:7, ▮◇:8, △△:3} — and still cannot submit, because 24 orderings are available and the lock takes one. Conversely the neighbour's four glyphs are inert without the map: they name shapes, and shapes are worth nothing until someone has paired them to stations.

The gauges are labelled with SYMBOLS ONLY, deliberately never named — which is already the room's canon. That means the key CANNOT be dictated as a code. The neighbour has to describe shapes down the voice call ("a filled bar then a diamond, then a circle with a bar...") and the Engine player has to match the description against four glyph faces on the wall and push back when it's ambiguous. That is the ROOMS.md "shapes, not codes" mechanic doing real work: a transcript of this key is close to useless, so it resists the alpha-gamer collect-everything strategy in a way a number never can.

Contract fit in server/puzzles.js: this is a new type alongside cipher/sequence, with key = { kind: 'manifold', value: '▮◇ ○▮ △△ ◇▲', label: 'MANIFOLD ORDER' }. wouldSolve() needs a branch, but the invariant is naturally safe — a manifold key can only solve a manifold prompt, and there is exactly one Engine Room per session, so no chamber can ever hold the key to its own prompt. The station digits and glyph assignment must be shipped to the client (they are painted on the room, so nothing secret leaks); only VENT_STATIONS and the resulting answer stay server-side.
seededValues: T, the loop period, from {16, 18, 20, 22} seconds — sets slug speed, and flywheel/piston rates derive from it (T/3 per revolution, T/9 per stroke) so every motion in the room stays commensurate

STATION_DIGITS: an ordered 6-tuple, a random permutation of six digits drawn from {2,3,4,6,7,8,9} — painted north-to-south into the glow-bed canvas. Excludes 1/0/5 so nothing collides with I/O/S when read aloud
GLYPHS: four two-glyph symbols drawn from a pool of eight (◇▲ ○▮ △△ ▮◇ ▲○ ▮▮ ◇◇ △▮), assigned to the four gauge positions north-to-south, rebuilt into the existing gauge atlas

VENT_STATIONS: an injective map gauge(0-3) -> station(0-5). Constraint: the four chosen stations, listed in gauge wall order, must not be monotonic increasing or decreasing — otherwise the banks-line-up guess wins without observation
MANIFOLD_ORDER: the permutation of the four gauges the answer must be typed in — this is the neighbour's key. Constraint: not the identity and not the exact reverse
PISTON_ORDER: a permutation of the six housings giving the firing stagger (cosmetic, but reseeded so the travelling wave down the bank differs per session)
NEEDLE_REST: four rest angles in the left third of each dial, so the idle pose differs per gauge and the slam has visibly different throw on each

geometryChanges.change: NEW — coolant slug. One thin MeshBasicMaterial plane, 0.34 x 0.5m, lying flat at y = -0.78 (0.02 above the glow bed), colour #eaffb0, x fixed at +2.9, z = -3.3 + 6.6 * frac(elapsed / T). Unlit on purpose, matching the glow bed's existing rationale: the coolant IS a light source and must not be shaded. Recirculates through the dark north end of the pit so the wrap reads as plumbing, not a jump cut.
geometryChanges.cost: +1 draw call, 0 lights, 0 textures — the entire render budget of this puzzle

geometryChanges.change: Station lane + numerals painted into makeGlowBedTexture(). A dark 0.5m-wide channel running north-south at x=+2.9 with six tick marks and six dark stencilled digits (~48px on the 512 canvas = 0.68m in world) at z = -2.25 + 0.9k. Uses the texture's existing dark-channel-plate idiom, so it reads as machinery rather than signage. Requires the function to take (seed, digits) instead of its hardcoded lcg(6673).
geometryChanges.cost: 0 draw calls, 0 new textures — repaints an existing canvas

geometryChanges.change: Gauge needles: replace the sin() wobble with rest-plus-vent. For gauge g let u = signed distance in seconds from elapsed to its vent time, wrapped to (-T/2, T/2]; angle = rest + (full - rest) * K(u), where K ramps 0->1 over u in [-0.6,-0.25], holds 1 for |u| <= 0.25, ramps back over [0.25,0.6], and is 0 beyond. The 0.5s pin is centred on the slug crossing the numeral, so at full deflection the slug is within +/-0.09m of the mark — dead on it, with 2.455s of clear air to the next station.
geometryChanges.cost: 0 draw calls — same 4-instance InstancedMesh, arithmetic change only

geometryChanges.change: BUG, and a hard-constraint violation: engine-room.js line 677 does flywheel.rotation.y += dt * 0.9, which accumulates per frame, so it depends on frame history and drifts between clients. The strobe and the glow-bed colour both derive from it, so the room's key light is currently non-deterministic. Must become flywheel.rotation.y = elapsed * (2*PI*3/T) — three revolutions per loop, giving exactly 18 strobes per loop so the machine counts itself and a struggling player can time vents in flashes.

Re-time the pistons from sin(elapsed*4.2 + i*1.05) to period T/9 (2.0s at T=18) with the stagger taken from the seeded PISTON_ORDER. Not load-bearing for the answer — but every period in the room must divide T, or an incommensurate motion manufactures slow drifting near-coincidences that look like the pattern and never resolve. That is the cruellest possible bug in a timing puzzle and it would be invisible in review.
geometryChanges.cost: 0 draw calls; 6 matrix writes per frame as today

geometryChanges.change: Accessibility blocker to resolve before build: engine.js line 681 reads `if (!reducedMotion) mounted?.update?.(dt, clock.elapsedTime)` — with reduced motion on, update() never runs, so a reduced-motion player sees a frozen room and CANNOT solve any timing puzzle. Needs a path: keep calling update() with a stepped/slowed clock, or have the Fragment panel offer a static trace log of one loop.
Optional polish: give the needle InstancedMesh an instanceColor so the venting gauge brightens as it slams. Sells 'this one is talking' without a per-gauge material.

fragmentBrief:
COOLANT LOOP B — MANIFOLD TRACE

One slug of hot coolant runs the east channel, past six
numbered stations, once per loop.

Four manifold gauges. No names, no units. Each one vents
exactly once per loop — and not one of them vents at random.

Submit four station numbers, in the MANIFOLD ORDER your
neighbour holds. Two stations never come up.
exampleWalkthrough:
SEED: T = 18s. STATION_DIGITS north-to-south = [7, 3, 9, 2, 8, 4]. GLYPHS by gauge (north-to-south) = G1 ○▮, G2 ◇▲, G3 ▮◇, G4 △△. VENT_STATIONS = G1->3, G2->0, G3->4, G4->1 (live stations 3,0,4,1 — non-monotonic; stations 2 and 5, digits 9 and 4, are never used). MANIFOLD_ORDER = ▮◇ , ○▮ , △△ , ◇▲.

Station arrival times, t_k = T*(z_k + 3.3)/6.6:
  station 0 (digit 7) at 2.864s   station 3 (digit 2) at 10.227s
  station 1 (digit 3) at 5.318s   station 4 (digit 8) at 12.682s
  station 2 (digit 9) at 7.773s   station 5 (digit 4) at 15.136s

WHAT THE PLAYER DOES.
Loop 1, first pass. She backs into the west aisle beside the pistons because that is the only spot where the gauges and the pit are both in frame. At t=2.9s the ◇▲ needle slams right. She was watching the wall, not the floor, and misses where the slug was. At 5.3s △△ slams. At 10.2s ○▮. At 12.7s ▮◇. Four vents, no pattern — they are not evenly spaced and they are not in wall order.

Loop 2. She watches the floor instead and counts: the slug crosses 7, then 3, then 9, then 2, then 8, then 4, and vanishes off the north end. Six numbers, 2.5s apart, same every time.

Loop 3. She holds both in view and catches it: the slug is sitting square on the 7 at the exact moment ◇▲ slams. Nine seconds later the slug is on the 2 and ○▮ slams. That is the moment — the gauges aren't measuring anything, they are calling out the station under the slug. She confirms across loop 4 and writes the map:
  ○▮ -> 2    ◇▲ -> 7    ▮◇ -> 8    △△ -> 3
and notices 9 and 4 never get called, which is how she knows she has all four and hasn't mistimed one.

THE CALL. She still cannot type it. Over the voice call the Vault player reads her MANIFOLD ORDER, and it is four shapes, not four numbers: "filled bar then a diamond. Then a circle with a bar after it. Then two triangles. Then a diamond with a triangle." She has to look at the four gauge faces and argue one of them out — "hollow circle or filled?" — before she is sure of the second.

  ▮◇ -> 8    ○▮ -> 2    △△ -> 3    ◇▲ -> 7

ANSWER TYPED: 8237

VERIFY THE INVARIANTS. The key alone is four glyphs — no digits, unusable. The observation alone is a four-entry map with 24 possible orderings — unusable. Reading the lane straight off gives 739284, which is not the answer and never can be. Brute force from the six visible digits is 6P4 = 360 ordered strings at a 30s lockout each, about three hours.
difficultyNotes:
WHY A 13-YEAR-OLD GETS THERE. The rule is one sentence with no vocabulary in it: the needle jumps when the light is on that number. No arithmetic, no cipher, no shift, no real-world knowledge. Every element is a physical object doing a visible thing, and the answer is literally painted on the floor in digits — the player is never asked to compute a value, only to notice which four of six get chosen and by whom. The failure states are all recoverable: the loop repeats forever, a missed vent costs 18 seconds, and there is no penalty for watching.

WHAT STOPS IT BEING INSTANT.
1. The two-surface problem. The cause is on the floor and the effect is on the wall, and a player's instinct in a room full of gauges is to stare at the gauges. Nearly everyone burns a loop or two watching only one surface. Finding the west-aisle standing spot where both fit in frame is itself a small discovery.
2. The four vents are not evenly spaced (2.9s, 5.3s, 10.2s, 12.7s here) and their order does not match wall order, so the first loop actively looks like noise.
3. Two dead stations. A player who assumes all six count builds a six-digit string and is wrong, and the wrongness is quiet — nothing tells them except the lock.
4. The pistons are a real, stable, seeded rhythm attached to nothing. They reward attention with a pattern that goes nowhere. This is the honest kind of red herring: genuinely there, genuinely regular, genuinely irrelevant.
5. The key is shapes. It cannot be dictated in four seconds; it has to be described, questioned and confirmed, and the two players will get one glyph wrong at least once.

CALIBRATION. Roughly 60-90 seconds of watching to build the map (3-4 loops), plus the glyph conversation. Total 2-4 minutes for a crew that is talking to each other, longer for one that isn't — which is the correct failure mode for this game.

RISK I'D FLAG BEFORE BUILD. The numerals sit under the grating and roughly 53% of each is covered by bars. Because the grating is a zero-thickness alpha-tested plane, the coverage is parallax-stable and the 0.09m bar pitch is far finer than the 0.68m digit, so it should read like a screen door — but 2 vs 7 through a grid on a school laptop is exactly the kind of thing that survives design review and dies in playtest. Test the digit set on target hardware before locking the pool; the fallback is dropping to four stations at 1.2m spacing with larger numerals.
